clinicalScope: Sickle Cell Disease (HbSS genotype) in children and adults presenting to low‑resource East African hospitals
title: Sickle Cell Disease
subject: Medicine
summary: Sickle cell disease is an inherited blood disorder where red cells become rigid and sickle‑shaped, causing painful crises, anemia and organ damage. In East Africa it is common, often presents with hand‑foot swelling in toddlers, and carries high infection risk because the spleen stops working.

sections.p: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a group of autosomal recessive hemoglobinopathies, the most severe being homozygous HbSS. Prevalence in sub‑Saharan Africa reaches 1‑2 % of newborns, making it a leading cause of childhood morbidity and mortality.
b: Autosomal recessive inheritance; not X‑linked.
HbSS accounts for ~70 % of cases in East Africa.
Carrier frequency (HbAS) up to 20 % in some regions.
High mortality without newborn screening and prophylaxis.

sections.h: Causes and risk factors, most likely first
sections.p: The primary cause is inheritance of two sickle β‑globin genes (HbS). Modifiers and triggers influence severity.
b: HbSS genotype – two sickle alleles.
Co‑inherited α‑thalassaemia – reduces HbS concentration, milder disease.
Dehydration, hypoxia, acidosis, extreme temperature – precipitate vaso‑occlusion.
Infections (malaria, pneumococcus, HIV, TB) increase sickling risk.
Low socioeconomic status → poor nutrition, limited access to care.

sections.p: Polymerisation of deoxygenated HbS distorts red cells, leading to hemolysis and vaso‑occlusion.
b: HbS polymerises when O₂ tension falls → rigid, sickle‑shaped RBCs.
Rigid cells obstruct microvasculature → ischemia, pain crises.
Chronic hemolysis releases free hemoglobin, scavenges nitric oxide → vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension.
Repeated splenic infarction → functional asplenia, Howell‑Jolly bodies on smear.
End‑organ damage from cumulative ischemia (kidney, brain, bone).

sections.p: Clinical manifestations evolve with age; early signs are characteristic, later complications dominate.
b: Dactylitis (painful swelling of hands/feet) before age 2 – most common first presentation.
Recurrent vaso‑occlusive pain crises in long bones, chest, back.
Chronic hemolytic anemia → fatigue, pallor, jaundice, gallstones.
Functional asplenia → fever is an emergency (risk of encapsulated sepsis).
Growth retardation, delayed puberty, priapism in males.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and exam quickly identify crisis type and red‑flag complications.
b: Ask about pain pattern, triggers (cold, dehydration, infection), frequency of crises per year.
Enquire about recent fever, respiratory symptoms, urinary changes, neurologic deficits.
Examine for tenderness over long bones, swelling of hands/feet, splenomegaly (early) or absent spleen (later).
Check for jaundice, hepatomegaly, signs of heart failure, and respiratory distress.
Measure vitals; note tachypnea, hypoxia, or hypotension indicating severe crisis.

sections.p: Consider other causes of anemia, bone pain and fever common in low‑resource settings.
b: Acute osteomyelitis (often Staph aureus) – localized warmth, pus, elevated CRP.
Septic arthritis – joint effusion, limited range of motion.
Thalassaemia major – microcytic anemia, absent sickle cells on smear.
Malaria – episodic fever, parasites on thick smear.
Acute leukemia – pancytopenia, blasts on peripheral smear.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Prioritise tests that are available; interpret results in the context of limited resources.

t.a: Complete blood count (CBC) with reticulocyte count
t.b: Quantifies anemia severity and marrow response; Hb < 8 g/dL with retic > 5 % suggests hemolysis.
Shows sickle‑shaped RBCs, target cells, Howell‑Jolly bodies; confirms diagnosis when electrophoresis unavailable.
Gold standard; HbS ≥ 50 % confirms SCD. If unavailable, rely on smear + clinical picture.
Elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin with low haptoglobin indicate active hemolysis.
Detects infiltrates or pleural effusion in acute chest syndrome; if X‑ray not available, use clinical criteria (fever + new cough + hypoxia).
Detects hemoglobinuria during vaso‑occlusive crisis; proteinuria signals early renal involvement.

sections.p: Severity guides intensity of disease‑modifying therapy and follow‑up.
b: Mild: ≤2 pain crises/year, no organ damage, Hb ≥ 8 g/dL.
Moderate: 3‑5 crises/year or early organ changes (splenomegaly, mild renal dysfunction).
Severe: >5 crises/year, stroke, pulmonary hypertension, renal failure, or Hb < 6 g/dL.
Use the WHO SCD severity classification adapted for low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in East Africa can mask or worsen SCD.
b: Malaria infection – increases hemolysis, may mimic crisis.
HIV – immunosuppression raises sepsis risk; drug interactions with hydroxyurea.
Tuberculosis – chronic cough may be confused with acute chest syndrome.
Nutritional deficiencies (iron, folate) – exacerbate anemia.
Traditional herbal remedies – can cause nephrotoxicity or interfere with hydroxyurea.

sections.p: Treat acute crises, prevent complications, and modify disease course.
b: Acute pain crisis: aggressive oral/IV analgesia (opioids if needed), hydration 1.5‑2 L/m²/day, oxygen if SpO₂ < 94 %.
Fever in SCD: treat as emergency – give parenteral ceftriaxone (or ampicillin‑gentamicin if unavailable) after cultures, give IV fluids, monitor vitals.
Acute chest syndrome: broad‑spectrum antibiotics, oxygen, incentive spirometry, consider blood transfusion if Hb < 7 g/dL.
Hydroxyurea (if available): increases HbF, reduces crises; start after baseline CBC, monitor for cytopenia.
Vaccination & prophylaxis: pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, Hib, meningococcal vaccine, penicillin prophylaxis until age 5.
Transfusion therapy: simple transfusion for severe anemia or stroke; exchange transfusion if resources allow.
Education: hydration, temperature avoidance, prompt fever evaluation.
Acute chest syndrome – fever, chest pain, hypoxia; mortality high without ICU.
Splenic sequestration – sudden abdominal fullness, Hb drop > 2 g/dL, tachycardia.
Stroke – focal neurologic deficit, seizures; urgent neuro‑imaging if possible.
Severe sepsis – fever, hypotension, altered mental status; start empiric antibiotics immediately.
Renal failure – oliguria, rising creatinine; consider dialysis if available.

sections.p: Pregnant women, infants, and adults have distinct needs.
b: Infants (<6 months): start penicillin prophylaxis after newborn screen; avoid aspirin.
Pregnancy: increased vaso‑occlusive risk; monitor for pre‑eclampsia, fetal growth restriction; transfuse if Hb < 7 g/dL.
Adults: higher risk of pulmonary hypertension and leg ulcers; screen with echocardiogram if symptomatic.
Patients with HIV: adjust hydroxyurea dose, monitor CD4 count.
Travelers to malaria endemic areas: strict chemoprophylaxis and insect protection.

sections.p: Regular care dramatically improves survival; most deaths in low‑resource settings are preventable.
b: Annual review: CBC, renal & liver function, blood pressure, growth parameters.
Transcranial Doppler ultrasound (if available) for stroke risk in children.
Vaccination schedule adherence reduces sepsis mortality.
Hydroxyurea use cuts crisis frequency by ~50 % and improves survival.
Community education on hydration, fever management, and early clinic presentation.

sections.p: Certain labs may be falsely normal or abnormal in SCD.
b: Serum bilirubin may be mildly elevated chronically; a sudden rise suggests hemolytic crisis.
LDH can be high at baseline; trend rather than single value guides decisions.
Reticulocyte count may be low during aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19) despite chronic high counts.
Chest X‑ray may be normal early in acute chest syndrome; rely on clinical criteria.
Peripheral smear may miss sickle cells if patient is on hydroxyurea and HbF is high.

whenToSeekHelp: Fever > 38.5 °C in any child with SCD
New onset chest pain with shortness of breath or hypoxia
Severe abdominal distension with rapid heart rate

faq.q: Why does splenic function disappear in SCD?
faq.a: Repeated micro‑infarctions cause fibrosis and loss of splenic tissue, leaving the patient functionally asplenic.
No; it increases fetal hemoglobin and reduces crises but does not eradicate the sickle gene.

faq.q: What is the first step when a child with SCD presents with fever?
faq.a: Treat as sepsis: obtain cultures, start parenteral antibiotics, give IV fluids, and admit for observation.

exam: A 3‑year‑old with SCD presents with hand swelling and fever. What is the most likely diagnosis and immediate management? — Dactylitis; give analgesia, hydration, and start empiric antibiotics because fever in SCD is an emergency.

Explain how dehydration precipitates a vaso‑occlusive crisis. — Low plasma volume increases blood viscosity; sickled cells have less space to flow, promoting polymerisation and microvascular blockage.
Interpret a peripheral smear showing sickle cells, target cells, and Howell‑Jolly bodies. — Confirms SCD with functional asplenia; Howell‑Jolly bodies indicate absent splenic filtration.
A patient has Hb 6 g/dL, retic 12 %, LDH 800 U/L. What does this pattern indicate? — Severe hemolytic anemia with high marrow response; likely acute crisis or splenic sequestration.
How does hydroxyurea reduce pain crises? — Increases HbF production, which inhibits HbS polymerisation, decreasing sickling and vaso‑occlusion.
What are the red‑flag features of acute chest syndrome? — Fever, new pulmonary infiltrate, chest pain, hypoxia (SpO₂ < 94 %), and tachypnea.

A child with SCD develops sudden abdominal fullness and a drop in Hb from 9 to 6 g/dL. What is the likely complication and next step? — Splenic sequestration; give rapid IV fluids and consider blood transfusion.
Why is pneumococcal vaccination critical in SCD? — Functional asplenia impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms; pneumococcus is a leading cause of fatal sepsis.

Describe how you would differentiate an SCD vaso‑occlusive pain crisis from osteomyelitis in a low‑resource setting. — Pain crisis: diffuse bone pain, no localized warmth, normal CRP; osteomyelitis: focal tenderness, swelling, high CRP, possible sinus tract.
A patient on hydroxyurea has a CBC showing WBC 2 × 10⁹/L. What does this mean for therapy? — Possible myelosuppression; hold hydroxyurea and monitor counts before restarting.
What screening test predicts stroke risk in children with SCD? — Transcranial Doppler ultrasound; velocities > 200 cm/s indicate high risk.
Explain why a normal LDH does not rule out a hemolytic crisis in SCD. — Baseline LDH is often elevated; trends and accompanying clinical signs are more informative.
